newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Hanbo chief admits payments for election.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Hanbo chief admits payments for election.

text.p: The founder of South Korea's stricken Hanbo Group, in dramatic testimony broadcast live from a Seoul jail, told a parliamentary inquiry on Monday he had donated money to President Kim Young-sam's election campaign.
Chung Tae-soo told a hearing in jail, the first in South Korea's history, that he also contributed to political funds for leading members of ruling and opposition parties.
Hanbo was one of the great corporate success stories under Kim's administration, and the collapse of its steelmaking flagship in January uncovered corrupt links between the group and politicians.

Three of Kim's close associates, including a former cabinet minister, are on trial with Chung and six others in a bribery scandal in connection with the failure of Hanbo Steel Co, South Korea's second-largest steelmaker, under debts of $5.8 billion.
Commenting on a hot political issue, Chung said he donated up to one billion won ($1.12 million) to Kim's ruling party to help fund the 1992 presidential election.
But he said the contribution was legitimate as he was a member of the party's financial commitee.
When asked by parliamentarians if he made any donation for the presidential election, Chung said: "Yes. As a member of a financial commitee member, I contributed to the election fund."
Asked about the size of the donation, he said: "A political donation is limited to a maximum of one billion won."

Chung, wearing a light-blue prison uniform emblazoned with the number 2952, denied giving any money personally to Kim but admitted asking Kim's close associate, Hong In-gil, to help his company obtain bank loans.
Hong, among the 10 people on trial over the scandal, has been charged with accepting bribes from Chung.
Chung also admitted contributing political funds to a group of politicians but declined to give details, saying the issue was pending in his trial.
The hearing is part of a 45-day special probe by parliament into the biggest corporate failure in South Korean history.

It was arranged after opposition parties attacked an investigation by state prosecutors into the Hanbo failure as a whitewash that failed to bring to justice major players in the loans-for-kickbacks scandal.

Chung apologised to the people for a major shock to the economy caused by Hanbo's failure but said policymakers and bankers must also be held responsible for letting it default on debt payments months before a new mill was due to be launched.
"It was like pulling out normal teeth. I told them this could cause harmful side effects which might lead to the death of the whole body," he said in clearly angry voice.
Chung, often closing his eyes, denied bribing politicians to secure loans far in excess of its capacity to repay them.
"If we had 300 billion won more in loans, there would not have been any defaults and the Hanbo project would have been successful," he said.
Chung, with his head upright and speaking in a firm tone, denied charges that he used 213.6 billion won of Hanbo debt for purposes unrelated to investment or operating the company.
"The misunderstanding arose because of interest payments. About 1.5 trillion won was paid as interest," he said.

Chung often responded to sensitive questions by answering: "I don't know", "I can't remember", and "I cannot tell you", prompting protests by seven legislators who warned of legal steps for "contempt of parliament".

Prosecutors, who reopened their probe into the Hanbo scandal last month, said they were looking into suspicions that President Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, accepted kickbacks and pressured banks to offer loans to Hanbo.
Kim Hyun-chul is scheduled to testify later this month before the National Assembly's hearing.
